"Score each option 1-5 on each criterion. There is no NA: a field that says \"none\" or \"none known\" scores 1. Give each score a reason of at most 20 words. Score from the quantities, sources and gaps the option names; ignore verdict words such as COMPUTE-BOUND or NOT COMPUTE-BOUND. Also label each option SAME, ADJACENT or ELSEWHERE against the root question, with a reason: SAME if it asks the root question or a sub-question of it, ADJACENT if it has the root's subject but asks a different question, ELSEWHERE if its subject is different. Decide the subject from the title and summary; count root_link only if the summary itself describes the root question's object of study. Do not add up the scores. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Root question: What limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could that be fixed with a shit ton of GPU parallelism?
Criteria:
stakes: Suppose the question this option raises were answered, either way. 5 = a choice someone faces (what to buy, build, collect or scale next) turns on the answer, and either answer would move it; 3 = the answer would refine a belief but no choice turns on it, or one answer is already much more likely than the other; 1 = either answer is already expected, or nothing would change. Do not score how famous or important the field is, or how close it is to the root question.
open: Has published work already measured how the answer changes with the quantity compute buys here (models, layers, features, prompts or seeds analysed), across the range that $1,000 of Lambda on-demand GPU time (for scale, about 250 H100-hours) can reach? 5 = names the quantity and where published measurements stop (or that none exist), and the unmeasured range starts within that reach; 3 = the unmeasured range is reachable only through a smaller stand-in system, or published work already covers part of the reachable range; 1 = names no compute-bought quantity, or published work already covers everything within that reach, so the open range lies only beyond it.
internals: Does the summary name specific information the model's internals could carry that its outputs do not, and say why outputs miss it? 5 = names the information and why outputs miss it; 3 = names a general kind (features, a representation, a direction) without what it adds over outputs; 1 = names none.
reshape: Does the option name a part of the work that one answer waits on step after step, and a reason those steps might not have to run in order? 5 = names that chain and roughly how long it is; one answer leaves most of a GPU idle (a small state, or few runs needed, so copies side by side would not fill it); names what would have to be true of the system for the steps to be computed at the same time, in a form a cheap measurement could check; and no cited source already computes this chain in parallel for this system; 3 = names the chain and a way to restructure it, but one of these fails: the answer needs many independent runs, so copies side by side already fill the hardware; one run already fills a GPU; or no checkable condition is named; 1 = sequential says none, or the only parallelism is independent pieces (copies, a sweep, one job per GPU), or a cited source already computes this chain in parallel for this system. A method published for a different system does not lower this score. Do not score how famous the method or field is.
Options, one per line:
{\"id\":\"SAE feature extraction on learned rainfall-runoff models\",\"title\":\"Train sparse autoencoders on LSTM rainfall-runoff internals to expose representation-level equifinality\",\"summary\":\"Apply Goodfire-style sparse autoencoders to LSTM cell-state activations to recover a sparse dictionary of hydrological features, then ask which features are uniquely constrained by the runoff record and which interchangeable feature sets reproduce it, reframing the framer's equifinality as non-identifiability of internal features.\",\"root_link\":\"Bears on framer.md's equifinality claim (Beven & Binley: many parameter sets reproduce the hydrograph equally well) by asking the same question at the level of a learned model's internal features.\",\"compute_open\":\"More parallel compute buys layers and features analysed: SAE dictionaries reach millions of features on single layers of models up to Llama-3.3-70B (https://www.goodfire.com/blog/a-practical-guide-to-saes), while the only geoscience application stops at simplified MLPs and one precipitation classifier (https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jh000769); what is unknown above that is whether SAE features trained on deep LSTM cell states across the 531 CAMELS catchments stay monosemantic and hydrological rather than fragmenting.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is train LSTM -> dump cell-state activations -> train SAE -> autointerp labels -> correlate features with hydrological states (~5 serial steps); one answer needs one LSTM plus one SAE per layer, each well under a single GPU (an LSTM over 531 basins is single-GPU-scale, https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/23/5089/2019/). Only the within-layer chain must run in order (SAE training waits on that layer's activations), but SAEs for different layers are mutually independent and would run concurrently on separate GPUs if each per-layer SAE were the dominant cost, which is how Goodfire trained independent single-layer SAEs (layer 19 of the 8B model, layer 50 of the 70B model, https://www.goodfire.com/blog/sae-open-source-announcement), though no source has done this for LSTM hydrology models.\"}
{\"id\":\"Feature steering to map the identifiable manifold\",\"title\":\"Steer SAE features of a differentiable rainfall-runoff model to separate identifiable from equifinal directions\",\"summary\":\"Use Goodfire-style feature steering on a differentiable RR model (LSTM or autodiff GR4J) to measure which features causally change the simulated runoff and which do not, producing an intervention-based map of the posterior geometry that sets the autocorrelation time.\",\"root_link\":\"Bears on framer.md's core claim that the autocorrelation time and equifinality are properties of posterior geometry, by causally mapping which parameter/feature directions actually move the simulated hydrograph.\",\"compute_open\":\"More parallel compute buys features analysed: steering is published only for individual features or small top-k sets per output (https://www.goodfire.com/research/understanding-and-steering-llama-3), even though SAE dictionaries reach millions of features (https://www.goodfire.com/blog/a-practical-guide-to-saes); what is unknown above that is whether exhaustively steering a full dictionary recovers the complete identifiable-versus-equifinal direction set or whether sparse causal coverage already suffices.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is train differentiable RR model -> train SAE -> gradient attribution ranks features -> steer each feature and re-run the forward model to score the likelihood change -> assemble the identifiable manifold (~5 serial steps); the answer needs one forward run per (feature, steering-strength) pair, thousands of tiny runs that together barely load one GPU. Attribution must precede steering, but the per-feature steering measurements are fully independent and could be batched/vectorized across the dictionary, paying off only if the dictionary is large enough that the batch saturates the GPU; the nearest source that batched controlled interventions is SAE-V (https://arxiv.org/html/2502.06755v1).\"}
{\"id\":\"Active-subspace reparameterization of the calibration\",\"title\":\"Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain\",\"summary\":\"Identify the few data-informed directions along which the forward model varies (the active subspace) and run MCMC only on those while sampling the prior elsewhere, the non-neural, interpretability-flavored cousin of feature extraction that directly attacks the autocorrelation time through reparameterization rather than hardware.\",\"root_link\":\"Bears on framer.md's conclusion that the real lever on long chains is reparameterization or better samplers rather than more cores, by supplying exactly such a reparameterization.\",\"compute_open\":\"More parallel compute buys gradient samples used to estimate the active subspace: published demonstrations stop at M=300 gradient samples recovering a dominant one-dimensional subspace (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.04190) and at a 100-dimensional forward model with a two-dimensional active subspace (https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127); what is unknown above that is whether a single linear subspace still captures RR posteriors carrying the artificial multimodality from cheap integrators (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648).\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is draw M gradient samples (two forward evaluations each by finite difference, or one adjoint pass) -> average the outer products into the active-subspace matrix -> eigendecompose -> run MCMC on the active variables only (~4 serial steps); the answer needs M gradient samples plus one MCMC chain, and one GR4J forward is so cheap that a single GPU stays nearly idle. The M gradient samples are mutually independent and only the active-variable MCMC must run serially, so the samples could run in parallel if the forward model were expensive enough to justify it; the nearest source that tried this is Constantine, Kent & Bui-Thanh's active-subspace-accelerated MCMC (https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127).\"}
